title: Seeds and Germination
tagline: Inside a bean seed and a maize grain, what monocot and dicot seeds hold, and how a seed starts growing again.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every seed structure, comparison and germination type below is standard seed biology. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A seed is a ripened ovule containing a dormant embryo, a store of food and a protective coat, and this chapter treats it as three parts in that order. It works through the dicotyledonous bean seed, identifying the testa, hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons and the three parts of the embryo, then the monocotyledonous maize grain, where the fruit wall and seed coat are fused and a single cotyledon called the scutellum sits against a large starchy endosperm. The two are then compared directly, because the monocot against dicot contrast is the most examinable point in the chapter. The final section covers germination itself: the conditions a seed needs, the sequence of events during resumption of growth, and the difference between hypogeal and epigeal germination.

learningOutcomes: Draw and label a dicotyledonous bean seed and state the function of each part.
Describe the structure of a maize grain and identify it as a monocotyledonous seed.
Compare monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous seeds in terms of the features an examiner expects.
State the conditions needed for germination and distinguish hypogeal from epigeal germination.

blocks.text: Soak a dry pea or bean overnight, peel off the outer covering, and the seed separates into two thick halves with a small embryo attached to one of them. The outer covering is the seed coat or testa, which is tough and water-resistant and protects the seed in the soil; it is pierced at two points. The scar where the seed was attached to the pod wall by the funicle is the hilum, and just beside it is a small pore, the micropyle, through which water enters the seed and air is exchanged. On the concave face of one cotyledon lies the embryo in three parts. The plumule is the first shoot, bearing a tiny feathered young leaf, and it will become the shoot system of the seedling. The radicle is the embryonic root, which emerges first during germination and anchors the seedling. Between them is the hypocotyl, the region that will elongate and lift the cotyledons. The two cotyledons themselves are not leaves: they are the seed leaves that absorbed the endosperm during development and now hold the food reserve that feeds the embryo until it can photosynthesise.

items.meaning: The tough outer seed coat that protects the embryo from mechanical damage, disease and water loss.
The scar left on the seed coat where the funicle attached it to the pod wall.
A small pore in the seed coat that allows water and air to enter, and through which the radicle later emerges.
A seed leaf; two are present in a dicot and one in a monocot, and it stores or absorbs food for the embryo.
The embryonic shoot with its tiny leaves, which develops into the shoot system.
The embryonic root, the first structure to emerge during germination.
The part of the embryo axis below the cotyledons; its elongation lifts the cotyledons in epigeal germination.

items: The bean seed is non-endospermic: the endosperm is used up during development and the food lies in the two fleshy cotyledons.
The castor bean, by contrast, is a dicot that keeps a large endosperm in its seed — a dicot is not automatically endosperm-free.
The radicle always emerges before the plumule, because the seedling must anchor and absorb water before it can photosynthesise.
The testa must be broken by water uptake, which is why a seed will not germinate in dry soil.
Two cotyledons is the defining feature of a dicotyledonous seed, whatever else it looks like.
The plumule is the first true shoot; the structures it produces are leaves and stem, not roots.
The embryo is the miniature plant: plumule becomes shoot, radicle becomes root, hypocotyl becomes the connecting axis.
Soaking a seed softens the testa and starts the metabolic activity of germination within hours.

items.text: Split a soaked gram seed and the two halves fall apart; the small pale structure clinging to one half is the embryo, and the two thick halves are the cotyledons that fed it while it was dormant.
items.note: The embryo is easy to overlook because it is small and pressed against a cotyledon.

items.text: A seed buried too deeply fails to germinate even with water and warmth because the food reserve in the cotyledons is exhausted before the plumule reaches the light.
items.note: Shows that the stored food sets a limit on how deep a seedling can push through.

blocks.text: A maize grain is technically a fruit as well as a seed, because the fruit wall and the seed coat are fused into a single covering that cannot be separated. Beneath it lies the aleurone layer, a protein-rich outer part of the endosperm, and behind that the large starchy endosperm that makes up most of the grain. The endosperm is the food store and it is retained in monocot seeds rather than being absorbed into the cotyledon. On one side of the grain, separated from the endosperm by a thin layer called the epithelium, sits the single cotyledon known as the scutellum; it does not store food itself but absorbs the digested endosperm and passes it to the embryo. The embryo has a plumule enclosed in a sheath called the coleoptile, and a radicle enclosed in a sheath called the coleorhiza, with the hypocotyl and epicotyl joining them. The protective sheaths are the key monocot adaptation: they let the young shoot and root push through the abrasive soil without being damaged.

items: A maize grain is a monocotyledonous seed because it has one cotyledon, the scutellum.
The grain is a caryopsis: fruit wall and seed coat are inseparably fused, which is why it is both a fruit and a seed.
The endosperm is retained in monocot seeds, while most dicots transfer the food into their cotyledons.
The coleoptile protects the shoot and the coleorhiza protects the root; their names both mean sheath.
During germination the aleurone layer releases enzymes such as amylase that convert starch into soluble sugars.
The radicle comes out first, breaking through the coleorhiza, before the coleoptile emerges above the soil.
The scutellum has no chloroplast and does not photosynthesise; it is purely absorptive.
A grain of wheat, rice and maize all follow this same monocot plan with a persistent endosperm.

items.text: When barley grain is soaked for malting, the embryo signals to the aleurone layer, which releases amylase; the amylase breaks starch to sugar, and that sugar is what later feeds the brewing yeast.
items.note: The enzyme's role in the seed is the same role it plays in a beer or bread recipe.

items.text: Cut a maize grain lengthways and the boundary is visible: the pale starchy endosperm above, the yellowish scutellum pressed against it, and the embryo below with its pointed coleoptile.
items.note: The longitudinal cut is the only view that shows all three regions at once.

blocks.text: The two seed types differ on a handful of linked features, and the most reliable way to answer a comparison is to take them in order: number of cotyledons, where the food is kept, whether a covering sheath protects the embryo parts, and the venation and flower parts of the adult plant that follow from the same genetic programme. A monocot seed has one cotyledon, keeps its food in a persistent endosperm, and has the plumule and radicle enclosed in a coleoptile and coleorhiza; the adult plant has parallel leaf venation and flower parts in multiples of three. A dicot seed has two cotyledons into which the food has usually been transferred, has no coleoptile or coleorhiza, and gives an adult with net-veined leaves and flower parts in multiples of four or five. The terms themselves carry the key: monocot is short for one cotyledon and dicot for two.

blocks.caption: Monocotyledonous against dicotyledonous seeds
rows: Usually absorbed; castor is an exception
Relatively small against a large endosperm
Relatively large, filling most of the seed
In multiples of four or five

items: Ask first how many cotyledons there are: that single count decides monocot or dicot before any other feature is considered.
Endosperm retention is the second reliable cue — starchy white tissue remaining means endospermic, which in a seed this size usually means monocot.
The presence of a coleoptile or coleorhiza is exclusive to monocots and is worth quoting because few students remember it.
Both types contain the same three elements: a coat, a food store and an embryo.
A seed is dormant, not dead: it has low water content and very little metabolic activity until conditions change.
Dormancy lets a seed survive an unfavourable season and germinate when conditions suit the seedling.
The adult plant's venation and floral parts are as reliable for classification as the seed itself.
Some seeds need a specific trigger such as light, cold or even fire before dormancy breaks.

items.text: Onion is a monocot despite having a fleshy storage leaf rather than a typical seedling; counting the single scutellum in its grain settles it as a monocot.
items.note: Seed characters trump the appearance of the adult plant when the two seem to disagree.

items.text: Castor is a dicot that retains a large endosperm, so it cannot be sorted by the presence of endosperm alone; the two conspicuous cotyledons mark it as dicot.
items.note: This is the exception that proves the rule must be applied in the right order.

learn.title: Germination: conditions and the two types

blocks.text: Germination is the resumption of growth by a dormant embryo, and it requires four conditions. Water is essential both to soften the testa so the embryo can swell and break out, and as the medium in which the stored food is hydrolysed and transported; it is also the reactant in the digestion of starch. Oxygen must diffuse in for aerobic respiration, because the energy for the rapid cell division of germination comes from oxidising the stored food — this is why seeds sown in waterlogged soil rot instead of germinating. A suitable temperature, normally between about 20 and 30 degrees Celsius, is needed because the enzymes driving digestion and respiration have narrow working ranges. Food reserves in the cotyledons or endosperm supply the fuel until the plumule unfolds its leaves. During germination the radicle emerges first and grows downwards by positive geotropism, anchoring the seedling and starting water uptake; the plumule then turns upwards by negative geotropism and grows towards the light, and only after the leaves are green and expanded does the seedling begin to support itself by photosynthesis.

items: The four requirements are water, oxygen, a suitable temperature and a food reserve already present in the seed.
The radicle comes out first because the seedling must anchor itself and absorb water before it can photosynthesise.
The radicle grows downwards with positive geotropism and the shoot grows upwards with negative geotropism.
Light is not required by most seeds, which is why some can be buried; a few, such as lettuce, need light to break dormancy.
Seeds sown in waterlogged soil fail because oxygen cannot diffuse in, so the embryo cannot respire aerobically.
Respiration in germinating seeds is high, which is why a jar of sprouting grain feels warm.
The food reserve is exhausted if germination is delayed by deep sowing, so sowing depth matters.
Dormancy is broken by conditions such as after-ripening, alternating temperature, light or, in some species, fire.

items.text: Sow a bean and a pea side by side: in the bean the two cotyledons are pushed up above the soil and shrivel after a week, while in the pea they stay buried and the shoot rises between them.
items.note: A direct comparison that makes the hypocotyl against epicotyl distinction visible.

items.text: A laboratory test shows that germinating seeds placed in a sealed jar absorb oxygen and release carbon dioxide, while the same seeds in nitrogen do not germinate — proving that oxygen is a requirement rather than merely helpful.
items.note: The controlled comparison is what makes it evidence.

figures.caption: Figure: A dicotyledonous bean seed dissected
figures.description: Two cotyledons opened out like a book. On one half sits the embryo drawn as a small axis: a feathery plumule at the top, a hypocotyl in the middle, and a pointed radicle at the bottom, attached along the inner face of the cotyledon. On the outside of the seed the seed coat is shown with a distinct hilum scar and a small micropyle pore beside it.

figures.caption: Figure: A maize grain in longitudinal section
figures.description: A wedge-shaped grain cut lengthways showing the fused outer covering. The upper three quarters is starchy endosperm bounded outside by an aleurone layer. Against it lies the shield-shaped scutellum with its epithelium. Below, the embryo shows a plumule inside a coleoptile and a radicle inside a coleorhiza, joined by the hypocotyl.
labels: fruit wall fused with seed coat

figures.caption: Figure: Epigeal and hypogeal germination compared
figures.description: Two four-stage time series. Left, epigeal: the hypocotyl elongates and arches, drawing the two cotyledons up through the soil until they stand above ground, then the plumule unfolds between them. Right, hypogeal: the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons remain buried, and the shoot rises above the soil leaving the cotyledons underground.

keyPoints: A seed has three parts: a protective seed coat, a food store, and an embryo.
The bean seed has a testa with a hilum and a micropyle, two fleshy cotyledons, and an embryo of plumule, hypocotyl and radicle.
The bean is non-endospermic because the food was absorbed into the cotyledons; castor is an endospermic dicot.
The maize grain is a caryopsis in which the fruit wall and seed coat are fused, and it has one cotyledon called the scutellum.
The maize endosperm persists as the starchy store, and the aleurone layer releases enzymes that digest it during germination.
The coleoptile protects the plumule and the coleorhiza protects the radicle in monocot seeds.
Germination needs water, oxygen, a suitable temperature and an existing food reserve.
The radicle emerges first and grows downwards with positive geotropism; the shoot grows upwards with negative geotropism.
Epigeal germination carries the cotyledons above ground by elongating the hypocotyl, as in the bean.
Hypogeal germination leaves the cotyledons below ground and elongates the epicotyl instead, as in the pea and maize.
examFocus: A labelled seed diagram must show the embryo and both cotyledons; a labelled bean with no embryo drawn loses most of the marks.
Monocot against dicot comparisons are best answered from a table with cotyledon count as the first line, because it is the deciding feature.
In germination essays the word order matters: the radicle emerges first, then the plumule, and saying the shoot appears first contradicts the physiology.
Epigeal and hypogeal must be tied to which axis elongates — hypocotyl for epigeal, epicotyl for hypogeal — because naming examples alone earns only part of the credit.

questions.prompt: Which structure of a bean seed allows water to enter and through which the radicle later emerges?
questions.explanation: The micropyle is the small pore left in the seed coat where the integuments did not fuse. Water enters through it to soften the seed and restart metabolism, and because it is the thinnest point of the coat, the radicle pushes out through it during germination. The hilum is only the scar of attachment and the testa is the covering itself.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the hilum because both are surface features. The hilum is a scar; the micropyle is a functioning pore.

questions.prompt: In a maize grain the single cotyledon is called the __________, and the sheath that protects the young shoot as it pushes through the soil is called the __________.
questions.explanation: The scutellum is the flattened shield-shaped cotyledon pressed between the endosperm and the embryo; it absorbs the digested endosperm rather than storing food itself. The coleoptile is the hollow sheath enclosing the plumule, which shields the delicate shoot from abrasion as it grows upwards, while the coleorhiza performs the same job for the radicle.
questions.commonMistake: Swapping the coleoptile and the coleorhiza. The coleoptile is for the shoot and the coleorhiza for the root — root and radicle both begin with r.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes a bean seed?
questions.explanation: The bean has two cotyledons, so it is dicotyledonous, and at maturity its endosperm has been completely absorbed into those cotyledons, so it is non-endospermic — the two thick halves are the food store. Maize is monocotyledonous and endospermic, and castor is a dicot that is endospermic, which is why both halves of the description are needed.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming all dicots are non-endospermic. The castor seed retains endosperm and is the standard counterexample.

questions.prompt: State the four conditions necessary for germination and explain why each is required.
questions.answer: Water is needed to soften the testa so the embryo can swell and break out, and to act as the medium in which stored food is digested and transported. Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, which releases the energy the embryo uses for rapid cell division and elongation. A suitable temperature, normally about 20 to 30 degrees Celsius, is needed so that the enzymes of respiration and digestion work at their maximum rate. A stored food reserve in the cotyledons or endosperm is needed to supply that energy until the first leaves are green and can photosynthesise.
questions.explanation: Each condition must be paired with the reason it is needed rather than simply listed, because the list on its own is worth only partial credit. The food reserve is sometimes missed as a condition because students treat it as a property of the seed rather than a requirement, but it is asked for alongside the other three.
questions.commonMistake: Adding light as a universal requirement. Most seeds do not need light to germinate; only a minority have a light requirement.

questions.prompt: In which of these does germination take place with the cotyledons remaining below the soil?
questions.explanation: The pea shows hypogeal germination: the epicotyl elongates and carries the shoot upwards while the two cotyledons stay buried in the soil. The bean, mustard and cotton all show epigeal germination, in which the hypocotyl arches and draws the cotyledons up above the ground.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the bean and pea behave alike because both are common pods. They are the standard contrast: bean epigeal, pea hypogeal.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a maize grain, naming the parts and stating the function of each, and explain why it is called both a fruit and a seed.
questions.answer: A maize grain is covered by a single layer in which the fruit wall and the seed coat are fused, which is why it is both a fruit and a seed — this type of fruit is a caryopsis. Inside, the upper and larger portion is the starchy endosperm, the food store, whose outer aleurone layer is rich in protein and releases the enzymes that digest the starch during germination. Separated from the endosperm by an epithelium lies the scutellum, the single cotyledon, which absorbs the digested food and passes it to the embryo. The embryo consists of a plumule enclosed in a coleoptile, a radicle enclosed in a coleorhiza, and a hypocotyl and epicotyl joining them. Having only one cotyledon makes the grain monocotyledonous.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the covering, the store, the absorptive cotyledon and the embryo with both sheaths, each with a function. The fruit-and-seed point rests entirely on the fusion of the fruit wall with the seed coat, which must be stated explicitly rather than implied by calling it a grain.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the scutellum as a storage organ. It absorbs and transfers; the storage is done by the endosperm.

questions.prompt: A student sows a tray of seeds and waters them generously so that the soil stays waterlogged. After a week almost none have germinated and the seeds have started to rot. Explain the observation, state the condition that has been denied to the seeds, and suggest a change in practice that should improve germination.
questions.answer: Waterlogging fills the spaces between soil particles with water, so oxygen can no longer diffuse into the seed. The embryo needs oxygen for aerobic respiration, because the energy required to resume growth, digest the stored food and drive rapid cell division comes from oxidising that food. Without oxygen the seed cannot respire aerobically, growth does not resume, and the stagnant conditions allow fungal and bacterial decay, which produces the rotting. The condition denied is oxygen, not water — in fact water is present in excess. The remedy is to improve drainage by sowing in free-draining soil, watering thoroughly but allowing the surface to dry between waterings, and avoiding standing water in the tray, so that air can return to the seed.
questions.explanation: The observation must be explained by distinguishing water from oxygen, which is the heart of the question: too much water is precisely what removes the oxygen. Naming the condition, giving the physiological reason respiration fails, and then proposing a specific corrected practice together cover all four marks.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the seeds were overwatered and stopping there. Overwatering matters only because of the oxygen it excludes, and the question demands that link.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by epigeal germination and name the part of the embryo responsible for lifting the cotyledons above the ground.
questions.answer: Epigeal germination is the type in which the cotyledons are carried above the surface of the soil as the seedling develops — epi means above and ge means earth. It is brought about by the elongation of the hypocotyl, the region of the embryo axis below the cotyledons, which arches and draws the two cotyledons up through the soil. In the bean the raised cotyledons may turn green and photosynthesise briefly before they wither, once the first true leaves are established.
questions.explanation: Both parts of the question are required: the meaning of the term and the specific structure that causes the movement. Naming the hypocotyl is essential, and it is what separates an epigeal answer from a hypogeal one, where the epicotyl elongates instead.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the lift to the plumule. The plumule grows into the shoot; it is the hypocotyl that performs the lifting.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the correct sequence of events at the start of germination?
options: Plumule emerges, then radicle, then leaves expand
Radicle emerges first and grows downwards, then the plumule grows upwards
Cotyledons are absorbed before the radicle emerges
Roots and shoot emerge at exactly the same time
questions.answer: Radicle emerges first and grows downwards, then the plumule grows upwards
questions.explanation: The radicle always emerges first so the seedling can anchor itself and begin absorbing water, and it grows downwards because of positive geotropism. The plumule follows and grows upwards with negative geotropism towards the light, and the cotyledons are not absorbed until after the first leaves are functional and photosynthesis can take over.
questions.commonMistake: Placing the leaves first because they are the visible end product. They are the last of these events, appearing only after the root and shoot are established.

questions.prompt: The tough outer covering of a seed is the __________, while the scar where the seed was attached to the pod wall is the __________.
questions.explanation: The testa, or seed coat, is the protective outer layer that shields the embryo from mechanical injury, microbes and drying out, and it must be penetrated by water before germination can begin. The hilum is the small scar left on the coat where the funicle joined the seed to the placenta of the pod, and it is a permanent mark of attachment rather than a functioning structure.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'shell' or 'husk' for the first blank. Seed questions require the botanical term testa.

questions.prompt: Explain why a seed cannot be regarded as dead even though it appears inactive, and describe how dormancy benefits the plant. Give one example of a condition that must be met before dormancy is broken in a particular seed.
questions.answer: A seed is dormant rather than dead because the embryo inside is alive and intact: it has a low water content and a very low rate of metabolism, so it uses almost no food reserve and shows no visible growth, but its cells remain viable and can resume activity within hours of taking up water. Dormancy benefits the plant by allowing it to survive an unfavourable period — a cold winter or a dry season — in a protected, dispersible form, and by ensuring that germination is timed so the seedling emerges when conditions such as temperature and moisture are suitable for survival rather than at any random moment. Dormancy in some species is broken only after a period of cold stratification, in which the seed experiences chilled, moist conditions through winter, so that it cannot germinate during a warm spell in autumn that would be followed by killing frost.
questions.explanation: The answer must separate three ideas: why the seed is alive, how dormancy helps the plant, and a specific triggering condition. Life is argued from low but present metabolism and a viable embryo; benefit from survival and timing; and the example must be a real requirement rather than a vague statement that seeds wait for good conditions.
questions.commonMistake: Equating dormancy with death. The whole point of the first part is that a dormant seed is metabolically alive at a reduced level, not dead.
